lessons.title: How to quickly assess a vehicle's reusable parts and scrap value
lessons.body:
When a car arrives at your yard, you have about 15 minutes to decide its fate. Start with a quick walk-around. Check the tires: if they hold air and have more than 3mm tread, they're worth reselling. A good used tire sells for $10â$30 in most African markets. Next, look at the body panels. Doors, bonnets, and boots that are straight and rust-free can fetch $20â$50 each. Note any dents or rust holesâthose parts are scrap metal.

Open the bonnet. The engine block, cylinder head, and gearbox are high-value if they turn over. Use a breaker bar to turn the crankshaft pulley. If it moves freely, the engine might be rebuildable. A used engine can sell for $200â$800 depending on the model. Check the alternator, starter, and radiatorâthese are quick sellers. The catalytic converter is worth $50â$200 because of the precious metals inside. Remove it carefully.

Inside the car, test the seats, dashboard, and electronics. A working radio, speedometer cluster, or air conditioning compressor can be sold online or to local mechanics. Even switches and relays have value. Look for a spare tire and toolsâthose are easy money.

For scrap value, weigh the shell after removing reusable parts. A typical sedan shell weighs about 800â1,200 kg. Mixed steel scrap sells for $0.10â$0.25 per kg in many African countries. So a stripped shell might bring $80â$300. But if you leave valuable parts on it, you lose money. Always remove the battery (worth $5â$15 as a core), the alternator (test it first), and the wiring harness (copper content).

Keep a notebook or phone app to record what you find. After 10 cars, you'll know which models have the best parts. For example, Toyota Corollas and Nissan Sunnys have high demand for used parts. Peugeots and Renaults are common in West Africa, so their parts sell fast. Focus on what moves in your local market.

lessons.title: Draining and safely storing fluids: fuel, oil, coolant, and brake fluid
lessons.body:
Before you remove any part, drain all fluids. This prevents spills, protects you from burns, and lets you sell or reuse the fluids. You need: a drain pan (at least 10 litres), a funnel, clean containers with lids, and gloves. Work outdoors or in a well-ventilated area. Never smoke near fuel.

Start with fuel. Petrol is highly flammable. Use a hand pump or siphon hose to transfer fuel into a approved container. A typical car tank holds 40â60 litres. If the fuel is clean, you can sell it or use it in your own vehicle. If it's old or contaminated, store it separately for disposal. Never mix petrol with diesel. Label every container clearly.

Next, engine oil. Warm the engine for 2 minutes to thin the oil, then remove the sump plug. Let it drain into a pan. A car holds 3â5 litres of oil. Used oil can be sold to recyclers who refine it into base oil or burn it in industrial furnaces. In many African cities, used oil fetches $0.20â$0.50 per litre. Store it in sealed drums away from water.

Coolant (antifreeze) is toxic. Drain it from the radiator and engine block. A car holds 4â8 litres. Coolant often contains ethylene glycol, which is deadly to humans and animals. Never pour it on the ground. Store it in a labelled container. Some recyclers will take it, or you can dispose of it at a hazardous waste facility if available.

Brake fluid is also toxic and corrosive. Drain it from the master cylinder and brake lines. A car holds about 0.5â1 litre. Brake fluid absorbs water and becomes useless, so it cannot be reused. Store it separately and dispose of it properly. Never mix brake fluid with other fluids.

After draining, keep all containers closed and stored in a locked area. Spills should be cleaned with sand or sawdust, not washed into drains. Proper fluid handling protects your health, your community, and your business reputation.

lessons.title: Removing and disposing of batteries, tires, and catalytic converters
lessons.body:
Batteries, tires, and catalytic converters are the three most valuable and hazardous items to remove. Handle them with care.

Batteries: A lead-acid car battery contains sulphuric acid and lead. Wear gloves and eye protection. Disconnect the negative terminal first, then the positive. Use a battery carrier or a strong strapâbatteries weigh 15â25 kg. Never tilt a battery; acid can leak. Store batteries upright on a plastic tray in a covered area. A used battery is worth $5â$15 as a core, or you can sell it to a recycler who pays by weight (about $0.50â$1.00 per kg). Never break open a battery to drain acidâthat's illegal and dangerous.

Tires: Remove the valve core to deflate the tire, then use a tire iron or bead breaker to separate the tire from the rim. A used tire with good tread can be sold for $10â$30. Worn tires can be sold to a recycler who shreds them for rubber crumbs, or you can sell them as fuel to cement kilns (worth $1â$3 each). Never burn tires openlyâthe smoke is toxic. Store tires flat, out of the sun, to prevent cracking.

Catalytic converters: These contain platinum, palladium, and rhodium. A used converter can be worth $50â$200 depending on the model and condition. Use a reciprocating saw or angle grinder to cut the exhaust pipe on both sides of the converter. Wear a dust maskâthe ceramic honeycomb inside can release harmful fibres. Do not break the honeycomb to extract metals yourself; sell the whole converter to a reputable recycler. Some buyers will test it with a scanner. Keep a record of the serial number if visible. Store converters in a dry place.

After removal, dispose of any remaining hazardous waste properly. Check with local authorities for licensed recyclers. In many African countries, informal buyers exist, but always prioritise safe handling and legal disposal.

lessons.title: Handling refrigerants and other hazardous materials responsibly
lessons.body:
Air conditioning systems contain refrigerants like R-134a or R-12. These gases damage the ozone layer and contribute to global warming. Never vent refrigerant into the airâit's illegal in many countries and harmful. You need a refrigerant recovery machine. These cost $300â$800, but you can share one with other yards or hire a technician. Recovery captures the gas into a cylinder. Then you can sell the refrigerant to a licensed recycler or reuse it. A typical car holds 0.5â1 kg of refrigerant. If you can't recover it, take the vehicle to a licensed AC shop before dismantling.

Other hazardous materials include: brake fluid (already covered), transmission fluid, power steering fluid, and differential oil. These are similar to engine oilâdrain and store them separately. Transmission fluid can sometimes be reused if clean, but usually it's recycled. Power steering fluid is often flammable; keep it away from sparks.

Batteries contain lead and acidâsee previous lesson. Never drain acid into drains. Tires are not hazardous but burning them releases toxic fumes. Catalytic converters contain precious metals but also ceramic fibresâwear a mask when cutting.

Airbags are explosive. Never cut or puncture an airbag. If you must remove them, disconnect the battery and wait 30 minutes, then follow the manufacturer's procedure. Better yet, leave airbags to a professional. In many African countries, airbags are not reused due to safety concerns, but they can be sold to licensed demilitarisation companies.

Oil filters contain about 0.2 litres of used oil. Crush them and drain the oil into your used oil container. Fuel filters may contain petrolâdrain them too.

Always wear personal protective equipment: gloves, goggles, and a dust mask. Work in a ventilated area. Keep a fire extinguisher nearby. Store all hazardous waste in labelled, sealed containers. Check with your local environmental agency for disposal rules. Responsible handling protects your health, your community, and your business from fines.

lessons.title: Using a checklist to ensure no valuable part is missed
lessons.body:
A checklist prevents mistakes and maximises profit. Print or write this list and use it for every vehicle. Start with exterior: check all lights (headlights, taillights, indicators) â sell working bulbs and lenses. Mirrors, door handles, and grilles are quick sellers. Wipers and motors. Check the radiator grille and bumper for chrome or plastic trim. Wheels and tires: remove alloy wheels separately â they sell for $20â$50 each. Steel wheels are scrap.

Under the bonnet: alternator, starter, radiator, fan, condenser, compressor, power steering pump, water pump, ignition coil, distributor, ECU (engine control unit), sensors, and relays. The ECU can be worth $50â$200. Remove the battery. Check the wiring harness â copper wire sells for $2â$5 per kg. Remove the catalytic converter. Drain all fluids.

Interior: seats (if clean, $20â$100 each), dashboard, instrument cluster, radio, speakers, air vents, switches, seat belts, and carpet (if good). Check for a spare tire and tools. Remove the gear knob and handbrake lever. Glovebox and door panels. Even the rear-view mirror can sell.

Mechanical: engine and gearbox (if rebuildable), driveshaft, differential, axles, suspension struts, brake calipers, and discs. These are heavy but valuable. A used gearbox can fetch $150â$500.

After removing all reusable parts, weigh the shell. Then sort scrap metal: steel, aluminium (from engine blocks and wheels), copper (wiring), and brass (radiator). Aluminium sells for $1â$2 per kg, copper for $4â$8 per kg. Separate them for higher prices.

Keep a tally of parts sold and their prices. After 20 cars, you'll know which parts are worth your time. Update your checklist as you learn. For example, if you find that Toyota Hilux parts sell fast, add specific items like injectors and turbochargers. A good checklist turns a $200 scrap car into $800â$1,500 in parts and metal.

lessons.title: Preparing the vehicle for dismantling: lifting, supporting, and stabilizing
lessons.body:
Before you start removing heavy parts, you must lift and support the vehicle safely. Never work under a car held only by a jack. Use jack stands rated for at least 2 tonnes each. A typical car weighs 1,200â1,800 kg, so you need four stands. Place them under the chassis rails or subframe, not under the floor pan or plastic panels. For a unibody car, use the pinch welds or reinforced areas. If in doubt, consult the owner's manual for jacking points.

Use a hydraulic trolley jack (2â3 tonne capacity) to lift one end at a time. Lift the front first, place two stands, then lift the rear. Lower the jack slowly until the car rests on the stands. Shake the car gently to test stability. If it moves, reposition the stands. Chock the wheels that are still on the ground.

For extra safety, place large wooden blocks or spare tires under the car as a backup. Never use bricks or concrete blocksâthey can crumble. If you're removing the engine, support it with an engine crane or a strong beam before unbolting the mounts. Never let the engine hang by a single chain.

When removing suspension parts, the springs are under tension. Use a spring compressor or loosen the bolts slowly while the car is on the ground. Never cut a coil spring with a torchâit can explode.

Work on a flat, hard surface like concrete. Dirt or gravel can shift. If you're outside, be aware of soft ground after rain. Use plywood under the jack stands to spread the load.

Always wear steel-toe boots and gloves. Keep the work area clear of tools and debris. Have a fire extinguisher nearby. If you're working alone, tell someone. A safe dismantling job is a profitable oneâan injury costs you time and money. After the car is stable, you can start removing parts from the top down: battery, fluids, then engine, then suspension. Always follow your checklist.

quiz.q: What is a quick way to check if an engine might be rebuildable?
options: B) Turn the crankshaft pulley with a breaker bar
quiz.explanation: If the crankshaft turns freely, the engine is not seized and may be rebuildable.

quiz.q: What is the typical scrap value of a stripped sedan shell in many African countries?
quiz.explanation: A stripped shell weighs 800â1,200 kg and sells for $0.10â$0.25 per kg, giving $80â$300.

quiz.q: Which part is worth $50â$200 because of precious metals inside?
quiz.explanation: Catalytic converters contain platinum, palladium, and rhodium.

quiz.q: Why should you warm the engine before draining oil?
options: B) To thin the oil so it drains faster and more completely
C) To prevent oil from burning you
D) To make the oil easier to sell
quiz.explanation: Warm oil flows better, carrying more contaminants out.

quiz.q: How many litres of coolant does a typical car hold?
quiz.explanation: Most cars hold 4â8 litres of coolant in the radiator and engine block.

quiz.q: What is the danger of pouring coolant on the ground?
options: B) It is toxic to humans and animals
quiz.explanation: Coolant contains ethylene glycol, which is deadly if ingested.

quiz.q: Which fluid should never be mixed with others and cannot be reused?
quiz.explanation: Brake fluid absorbs water and becomes useless; it is also toxic and corrosive.

quiz.q: What should you do first when disconnecting a car battery?
quiz.explanation: Disconnecting the negative terminal first prevents short circuits.

quiz.q: How much is a used car battery typically worth as a core?
quiz.explanation: Core value for a lead-acid battery is usually $5â$15.

quiz.q: Why should you never burn tires openly?
options: A) It is a waste of rubber
B) The smoke is toxic and harmful
quiz.explanation: Burning tires releases toxic fumes and is illegal in many places.

quiz.q: What is the safest way to remove a catalytic converter?
options: A) Break the honeycomb with a hammer
B) Cut the exhaust pipe on both sides with a saw or grinder
D) Both B and C are safe
quiz.explanation: Cutting or unbolting are both acceptable; breaking the honeycomb releases harmful fibres.

quiz.q: Which refrigerant is commonly found in older car AC systems?
quiz.explanation: R-12 was used in older vehicles; R-134a is more common in newer ones.

quiz.q: Why must refrigerants be recovered rather than vented?
options: B) They damage the ozone layer and contribute to global warming
quiz.explanation: Refrigerants are potent greenhouse gases and ozone-depleting substances.

quiz.q: What should you do with an airbag before dismantling?
options: B) Disconnect the battery and wait 30 minutes
C) Remove it with a hammer
quiz.explanation: Airbags can deploy unexpectedly; disconnecting the battery and waiting reduces risk.

quiz.q: How much used oil does a typical oil filter contain?
quiz.explanation: Oil filters hold about 0.2 litres of used oil.

quiz.q: What should you wear when handling hazardous materials?
options: B) Gloves, goggles, and a dust mask
quiz.explanation: Gloves, goggles, and a dust mask protect against splashes, fumes, and particles.

quiz.q: What is the first item on a good vehicle assessment checklist?
options: B) Check exterior lights and trim
quiz.explanation: Starting with easily accessible exterior parts saves time and prevents damage.

quiz.q: How much can a used alloy wheel sell for?
quiz.explanation: Alloy wheels are valuable and typically sell for $20â$50 each.

quiz.q: What is the approximate value of a used ECU?
quiz.explanation: Engine control units are in demand and can fetch $50â$200.

quiz.q: Why should you separate copper wiring from other scrap?
options: B) Copper sells for a higher price per kg
D) Copper is easier to store
quiz.explanation: Copper fetches $4â$8 per kg, much more than steel.

quiz.q: What is the minimum weight rating for jack stands used on a typical car?
quiz.explanation: Each stand should be rated for at least 2 tonnes to safely support a 1.2â1.8 tonne car.

quiz.q: Why should you never use bricks to support a car?
options: B) They can crumble and cause the car to fall
C) They are hard to find
quiz.explanation: Bricks are brittle and can fail under load, leading to serious injury.

quiz.q: Where should jack stands be placed?
options: C) Under chassis rails or subframe
quiz.explanation: Chassis rails and subframes are strong enough to support the vehicle's weight.

quiz.q: What should you do before removing suspension parts?
options: A) Loosen bolts while car is on the ground
B) Cut the springs with a torch
quiz.explanation: Loosening bolts while the car is on the ground reduces tension on springs.

quiz.q: Why is it dangerous to cut a coil spring with a torch?
quiz.explanation: Heating a spring can cause it to release stored energy violently.

quiz.q: What is the best surface for working under a car?
quiz.explanation: Concrete is flat and stable, preventing jack stands from sinking.

quiz.q: What should you do if you must work alone under a car?
options: B) Tell someone your location and expected finish time
C) Use only one jack stand
quiz.explanation: Having someone check on you can save your life in an emergency.

quiz.q: What is the correct order for removing parts from a car?
quiz.explanation: Removing the battery first prevents electrical shorts, then drain fluids, then heavy parts.

quiz.q: How much can a used gearbox sell for?
quiz.explanation: A rebuildable gearbox typically sells for $150â$500 depending on model.

quiz.q: What should you do with a used tire that has good tread?
options: C) Throw it in a landfill
D) Cut it up for scrap
quiz.explanation: Good used tires have resale value and should be sold, not wasted.
